sources.note: Uses integrated-gradient token attribution, aggregated into per-segment strength and direction-consistency scores, to pick which segments of a long chain-of-thought an SFT run should compute loss on, masking the rest.
sources.title: Segment-Level Attribution for Selective Learning of Long Reasoning Traces

sources.note: DiffAdapt trains a small probe on a reasoning model's hidden state to classify each question as Easy/Normal/Hard and picks a matching prompt, temperature and token limit, cutting token use without retraining the model.
sources.title: DiffAdapt: Difficulty-Adaptive Reasoning for Token-Efficient LLM Inference

sources.note: FROST uses attention weights to identify and prune sentence-level 'reasoning outliers' from a reasoning model's chain of thought, reporting an average 69.68% token reduction and 26.70% accuracy gain over the base model on four maths benchmarks.
sources.title: FROST: Filtering Reasoning Outliers with Attention for Efficient Reasoning

sources.note: QFFT fine-tunes a short-CoT instruct model on Long CoT responses with the question deleted from every training example, so the model keeps its default concise reasoning and switches to reflective Long CoT only when it hits uncertainty or an error, cutting average tokens by roughly 50% at accuracy comparable to ordinary SFT.
sources.title: QFFT, Question-Free Fine-Tuning for Adaptive Reasoning

result.definition: The shorter spelling under which four archived papers - Segment-Level Attribution, DiffAdapt, FROST and QFFT - name the Minerva maths benchmark; none of them states what it contains, so the archive knows it only by where it sits in an evaluation suite. Segment-Level Attribution puts it out-of-domain, with GPQA-Diamond and OlympiadBench, against in-domain MATH500, AMC23 and AIME24, so it serves there as a generalisation check on compressed-CoT fine-tuning rather than as a training target. FROST's per-benchmark table places it near the hard end: Phi-4-Reasoning after outlier pruning reaches 27.16% on Minerva at 401.19 average tokens, against 93.11% at 154.33 tokens on GSM8K and 26.67% at 899.80 tokens on AIME24 - roughly AIME's accuracy for under half its budget. The archive holds a separate entry, 'Minerva Math', built from the papers that use the longer name; the two are near-certainly one benchmark, kept apart rather than aliased together because a wrong alias silently fuses two entities.
